L327@P6: l’angiotensine II)

L329@P6: immunofixation, et référer à l’allergologue dès que possible
L330@P6: L’angioedème héréditaire correspond en général à une mutation qui réduit la concentration ou l’activité du C1-
L331@P6: inhibiteur (qui inhibe le système du complément). 25% des mutations apparaissent de novo donc l’anamnèse
L332@P6: familiale peut être négative. 9
L333@P6: L’angioedème acquis correspond à une utilisation excessive du C1-inhibiteur (p.ex. en cas de lymphoprolifération)
L334@P6: ou à la présence d’auto-anticorps contre le C1-inhibiteur.
L335@P6: En cas de prise d’IEC / ARA2, l’éviction est nécessaire. En cas d’absence d’IEC / ARA2 ou si leur éviction ne
L336@P6: permet pas la résolution des symptômes, il faudra investiguer l’angioedème héréditaire ou acquis.1 En fonction
L337@P6: de la sévérité de la réaction, il faut considérer également l’éviction des inhibiteurs DPP4 (p.ex. sitagliptine,

L339@P6-7: aliskiren) et inhibiteurs m-TOR (p.ex. sirolimus, everolimus) qui peuvent interférer avec le système kininekalikréine).Service de médecine de premier recours

L0@P0: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis | May 2021
L1@P0: Key recommendations for clinical practice
L2@P0: • Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
L3@P0: • Recognise anaphylaxis based on:
L4@P0: o sudden onset and rapid progression of symptoms
L5@P0: o Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems
L6@P0: o skin and/or mucosal changes (flushing, urticaria, angioedema) –
L7@P0: but these may be absent in up to 20% of cases.
L8@P0: The diagnosis is supported if a patient has been exposed to an allergen known to
L9@P0: affect them.
L10@P0: • Treat life-threatening features, using the Airway, Breathing, Circulation,
L11@P0: Disability, Exposure (ABCDE) approach.
L12@P0: • Adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Give intramuscular (IM)
L13@P0: adrenaline early (in the anterolateral thigh) for Airway/Breathing/Circulation
L14@P0: problems.
L15@P0: o A single dose of IM adrenaline is well-tolerated and poses minimal
L16@P0: risk to an individual having an allergic reaction. If in doubt, give IM
L17@P0: adrenaline.
L18@P0: o Repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if Airway/Breathing/Circulation
L19@P0: problems persist.
L20@P0: • Intravenous (IV) adrenaline must be used only in certain specialist
L21@P0: settings, and only by those skilled and experienced in its use.
L22@P0: o IV adrenaline infusions form the basis of treatment for refractory
L23@P0: anaphylaxis: seek expert help early in patients whose respiratory and/or
L24@P0: cardiovascular problems persist despite 2 doses of IM adrenaline.
L25@P0: • Follow the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline
L26@P0: for the assessment and referral of patients suspected to have had
L27@P0: anaphylaxis. Specifically:
L28@P0: o All patients should be referred to a specialist clinic for allergy
L29@P0: assessment.
L30@P0: o Offer patients (or, if appropriate, their parent and/or carer) an
L31@P0: appropriate adrenaline injector as an interim measure before the
L32@P0: specialist allergy assessment (unless the reaction was druginduced).
L33@P0: o Patients prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors (and/or their
L34@P0: parents/carers) must receive training in their use, and have an
L35@P0: emergency management or action plan
L36@P0: • Further research is needed to better identify and treat patients at greatest
L37@P0-1: risk of severe anaphylaxis.Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis | May 2021
L38@P1: o Anaphylaxis reactions should be reported to the UK Anaphylaxis
L39@P1: Registry at www.anaphylaxie.net (to register, email
L40@P1: anaphylaxis.registry@ic.ac.uk).
L41@P1-2: o Follow guidance for reporting and debriefing of adverse events.Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis | May 2021
L42@P2: Summary of changes from previous guideline
L43@P2: This guideline replaces the previous guideline from Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK):
L44@P2: Emergency treatment of anaphylactic reactions – Guidelines for healthcare providers
L45@P2: (originally published January 2008, annotated July 2012 with links to NICE guidance).1
L46@P2: • Greater emphasis on intramuscular adrenaline to treat anaphylaxis, and repeated
L47@P2: after 5 minutes if Airway/Breathing/Circulation problems persist.
L48@P2: • A specific dose of adrenaline is now included for children below 6 months of
L49@P2: age.
L50@P2: • Increased emphasis on the importance of avoiding sudden changes in posture
L51@P2: and maintaining a supine position (or semi-recumbent position if that makes
L52@P2: breathing easier for the patient) during treatment.
L53@P2: • There are 2 algorithms:
L54@P2: o Initial treatment of anaphylaxis, with emphasis on repeating the dose
L55@P2: of adrenaline after 5 minutes and giving an IV fluid bolus if
L56@P2: Airway/Breathing/Circulation problems persist.
L57@P2: o Treatment of refractory anaphylaxis, defined as anaphylaxis where
L58@P2: there is no improvement in respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms
L59@P2: despite two appropriate doses of IM adrenaline.
L60@P2: • IV fluids are recommended for refractory anaphylaxis, and must be given
L61@P2: early if hypotension or shock is present.
L62@P2: • Antihistamines are considered a third-line intervention and should not be used to
L63@P2: treat Airway/Breathing/Circulation problems during initial emergency treatment.

L1476: ## THE DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS OF HAE
L1477: 
L1478: The differential diagnosis of HAE includes other angioedema endotypes, which may generally be associated with either the kinin system or mast cells.
L1479: Regarding the bradykinin-mediated angioedema (BK-AE) endotype, other potential causes should likewise be evaluated. These conditions include AAE-C1-INH from acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency, which is typically linked to autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disorders, and BK-AE with normal C1-INH, often caused by adverse drug reactions, such as to ACE inhibitors.【217†^{72}】^{,}【269†^{122}】^{,}【290†^{141}】 Other conditions that may mimic hereditary angioedema should be considered in the differential diagnosis.
L1480: These conditions include abdominal disorders such as intestinal obstruction, porphyria, and familial Mediterranean fever; localized edema syndromes such as Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome, Gleich’s syndrome, and contact dermatitis; and iatrogenic causes such as reactions to facial fillers, among others.【269†^{122}】^{,}【290†^{141}】^{,}【364†^{202}】
L1481: Patients with acquired angioedema due to C1-INH deficiency typically lack a family history of recurrent angioedema, and the condition usually presents later in life compared with HAE. The acquired form often is associated with underlying disorders such as lymphoproliferative diseases, including monoclonal gammopathy and lymphoma, or autoimmune conditions, possibilities that should be investigated.
L1482: As C1q levels are reduced in approximately 75% of cases and C1-INH autoantibodies are detected in 50%–60% of cases, testing is recommended when there is no family history of angioedema (【365†Table 3】).【366†^{203}】^{,}【367†^{204}】 ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema with a recurrent pattern and, due to their widespread use, represent the most common cause of emergency room admissions for BK-AE and a frequent differential diagnosis of HAE.
L1483: However, HAE can manifest in individuals who were previously asymptomatic and only become symptomatic after initiating these drugs, and C1-INH testing should be performed in such cases. Other medications, including DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) and neprilysin inhibitors, also can induce angioedema. Although angiotensin II receptor blockers have been implicated in some reports, their role in causing bradykinin induced angioedema remains controversial.【368†205】, 【369†206】, 【370†207】

L1497: Mast cell–mediated angioedema represents an important differential diagnosis due to its high frequency in the general population. It falls within the clinical spectrum of disorders such as chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), encompassing both phenotypes—those exacerbated and those not exacerbated by the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). NSAIDs may also induce isolated angioedema in the absence of urticaria among predisposed individuals.
L1498: Furthermore, IgE-mediated allergic reactions resulting from intermittent allergen exposure should be considered, as they may manifest as recurrent angioedema.【372†^{208}】
L1499: NSAIDs always should be investigated as a potential trigger in patients with or without chronic spontaneous urticaria.【372†^{208}】 However, up to 22% of HAE patients are reported to have been misdiagnosed with drug hypersensitivities, leading to delays in the diagnosis of HAE and adverse clinical outcomes.【373†^{209}】 Similarly, as noted, CSU is a common condition associated with recurrent angioedema, with or without pruritic wheals (hives).
L1500: Cases of patients affected by both CSU and HAE have been reported, and the presence of wheals should not automatically exclude a diagnosis of HAE. An observational, real-world study that included over 600 HAE patients showed that almost half had been previously misdiagnosed, leading to a median additional delay of 1.7 years to the correct diagnosis, and patients without a family history of HAE had an almost 60% higher likelihood of misdiagnosis.【374†^{210}】
L1501: HAE-CPN patients present a phenotype characterized by both angioedema and urticaria episodes. Carboxypeptidase N plays a crucial role in cleaving and degrading bradykinin, lys-bradykinin, and the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a. Mutations in CPN impair its function, leading to reduced degradation of bradykinin and anaphylatoxins, which may trigger both angioedema and urticaria attacks.
L1502: This scenario challenges the conventional belief that urticaria is not a characteristic feature of HAE, adding potential complexity to the presentation of the syndrome. The discovery of the HAE-CPN endotype has enhanced understanding of HAE while highlighting the need for a comprehensive approach to diagnosis and treatment.【190†^{49}】^{,}【375†^{211}】 However, these findings still require confirmation, and the global prevalence of HAE-CPN is unknown.

L1517: ## GENERAL PREEMPTIVE STRATEGIES
L1518: Although several triggers for HAE attacks have been identified, including physical trauma and injury, dental work, surgery and manipulation of the upper airway, endoscopy or other medical procedures, stress, infections, and intake of estrogens or ACE inhibitors, most episodes are spontaneous.【279†^{131}】^{,}【378†212】, 【379†213】, 【380†214】, 【381†215】, 【382†216】 An individualized risk assessment is warranted, as some patients could be affected by specific triggering factors, especially those related to emotional disturbance.【383†^{217}】 Measures to prevent exposure to frequent triggers include using hormonal contraception with progesterone-only pills (instead of estrogen-based products), avoiding ACE inhibitors if antihypertensive medication is required, following good dental care, receiving vaccines for influenza and COVID-19, and other routine infection-prevention measures.
L1519: Additionally, hepatitis A/B vaccination should be considered in patients who regularly receive plasma-derived products and fresh frozen plasma (FFP).【384†218】, 【385†219】, 【386†220】, 【387†221】, 【388†222】, 【389†223】 Of note, even though COVID-19 infection has been confirmed as a trigger for HAE attacks, infection severity and the mortality rate associated with this virus do not appear to be higher in HAE patients, and vaccination is considered safe.【389†223】, 【390†224】, 【391†225】, 【392†226】, 【393†227】
